threads.thread_goal: Align on current guest journey and agree on main pain points to fix first.

messages.text: Morning all. I have uploaded a first draft of the current guest journey map as A1, based on calls, lobby observations, and notes from T1. It covers from guest arrival at the driveway through to departure and luggage pick-up. Can porters please check if the steps match what really happens on shift, especially evenings and weekends, and add anything missing in this thread?

Thanks for sharing A1. Quick first look: the arrival side is close, but we usually have an extra step between greeting and tagging luggage where we confirm room readiness with front desk by radio if the guest is very early. That is not shown. Also, for departures, we often pre-stage luggage in the side corridor during busy check-out, which is not in the flow either.

Looking at A1 now. On late nights, guests sometimes go straight to the lift with their bags and only call us from the room if they need help. That path is not really shown. Should we add a branch for self-carry arrivals where we only get involved after a call or complaint?

I saw in A1 that after we tag luggage, it goes straight to room delivery. Sometimes we store it first if the room is not ready or guest goes to the bar. Maybe we should show that storage step, including the ticket we leave at the desk.

From my side, the departure part in A1 misses when guests call down from the room asking for help with bags but then come down themselves before we get up there. We end up looking for them and the luggage. Maybe that is one of the pain points we should flag.

I agree with the comments so far. A1 is a good base, but we should add: 1) early arrival room readiness check by radio, 2) luggage storage before room delivery, 3) self-carry arrivals where we only step in later, and 4) call-down for departure where guest comes down before we reach the room. Once we add those, the map will reflect what actually happens on busy shifts.

This is helpful. I will update A1 to add: early arrival room readiness check, optional storage before delivery, self-carry arrivals, and the missed-connection scenario on departure. Before I do that, are there any other missing steps, especially around when we call the contact centre or when you call us from the lobby?

One more: when a guest complains at the door about room not being ready or booking issues, we often call the contact centre first if front desk is tied up. That step is not in A1. It is a key moment because it can either calm things down or create more waiting if we do not reach anyone quickly.

Also, for group arrivals, we usually have a quick huddle with the group leader and front office before the buses arrive. That is not in A1. It is not every day, but when it happens it changes the flow a lot, especially for luggage tagging and storage.

Got it. I will add: door complaints leading to a call to the contact centre, and the group arrival huddle step. Once I update A1, I will post a short summary here so we can lock the current journey for T1. In parallel, can we start listing the main pain points you want us to tackle first?

For me, top pain point is when luggage tickets do not match what is in storage, especially on Sundays. Guests come down and we spend a lot of time searching. That is in A1 as a delay, but I think it should be one of the first things we fix.

Another big one is guests waiting at the driveway with no one greeting them when we are upstairs with bags. That is when complaints start and sometimes calls go to the contact centre. Maybe we need a clearer rule in the flow about who covers the door when one of us is away.

I would add the confusion when guests call from the room for bags at check-out and we already have a queue at the lobby. We end up juggling both and sometimes miss the promised time. That shows up in A1 as a delay but feels like a key issue.

Agree with the points raised. I would group the main pain areas as: 1) driveway greeting gaps, 2) luggage storage and ticket mismatches, and 3) coordination between lobby and room calls at peak times. If we focus on those first, we should see fewer complaints and shorter waits.

I support that list. Those three show up again and again in our shifts and in what guests tell us. Other issues like group arrivals are important but less frequent. We can still capture them in the map but maybe not in the first rollout focus.

Thanks all. I have now updated A1 with the extra steps we discussed: early arrival room check, optional storage, self-carry arrivals, door complaints leading to a call to us, group arrival huddle, and the missed-connection scenario on departure. Unless anyone spots a major gap today, I suggest we treat this as our agreed current journey for T1 and use the three pain points you highlighted as the first rollout focus.
Looks good to me. I do not see any missing steps now. Happy to work from this version of A1.
Same here. The updated A1 matches what we see on day, evening, and weekend shifts. Let us lock it and move on to the checklists and scripts using those three pain points as our priority.

threads.thread_goal: Co-create and finalise the porter arrival and luggage handling checklist.

messages.text: I have put together a first draft of the porter arrival and luggage handling checklist as A2, based on the updated journey in A1 and what is in T2. It covers greeting, tagging, storage, and room delivery. I am not fully sure where to place the door security checks so they do not slow us down. Can you all review and suggest changes, especially on order of steps and security?

Thanks for starting A2. Overall structure works, but I would tweak the order: 1) visual scan of driveway and entrance for safety, 2) greeting and quick check of booking name, 3) luggage count and tagging, 4) confirm room readiness, 5) decide storage vs direct delivery. For door security, I suggest we add a short reminder at the point where we escort guests to the lift and when we return to the entrance, so we do not leave the door unattended.

I agree with that sequence. On door security from T9, we need to be clear that if only one porter is on duty, we either: a) stay at the door and ask front desk to call for luggage help, or b) lock the luggage trolley in the side area and close the main door if we have to go upstairs briefly at night. Maybe A2 can have a small decision box for single-porter vs two-porters on shift.

In A2, step about tagging luggage mentions writing room number straight away. Sometimes we do not have the room yet, especially early arrivals. Could we change that to guest name and date first, then add room number once confirmed? That might reduce mismatches we saw in A1.

I noticed A2 does not say when we should call the contact centre or front office if we are delayed with luggage. Maybe we add a line: if delay will be more than 10 minutes, inform front desk or contact centre so they can update the guest.

From my side, A2 looks close. I support changing the tag rule to name first, room later, and adding the delay communication step. On door security, I would like us to align with the escalation matrix in A6 so that if there is any safety concern at the entrance, you know exactly who to call first. We can reference that in the checklist rather than repeating all details.

Thanks for the feedback. I will adjust A2 to: follow the new order suggested, change tagging to guest name and date first, add the 10-minute delay rule, and add a note to check A6 for safety concerns. For the single-porter vs two-porters decision, I might need help wording it simply so it fits on one page.

Happy to help. Suggest wording: if only one porter on duty, stay at entrance and ask front desk or contact centre for support with luggage. Only leave entrance unattended if instructed by manager or in emergency, following A6. That keeps it short and clear.

I like that. We should also add a quick door check when we return from a room: scan for unattended bags, people waiting, or anything unusual. It can be a one-line reminder in A2 so it becomes a habit without adding time.
Agree. That one-line reminder would help, especially on busy evenings when it is easy to miss a bag left by the door.

I have now updated A2 with: the new step order, name-first tagging, delay communication rule, single-porter rule, and the quick door scan reminder. Can you all confirm this sequence works for day, evening, and weekend shifts so we can treat it as our standard checklist for T2?

I have reviewed the latest A2. The steps and order make sense across shifts, and the door security checks are integrated in a way that should not slow service if we follow them. I am comfortable using this as our standard arrival and luggage checklist.

From the contact centre side, A2 looks good and aligns with A6 on who to call for safety issues. I approve the steps and the way door security is built in. We can now move on to training and make sure everyone is comfortable with the new flow.

threads.thread_goal: Agree on complaint handling script and escalation matrix across teams.

messages.text: I have posted draft versions of the complaint handling script as A3 and the escalation matrix as A6, both linked to T3, T4, and T6. The script has opening, probing, resolution, and closing steps, and the matrix shows who to contact by issue type and time of day. Can porters review and tell me if the wording feels natural at the door and if the escalation paths match what actually works on shift?

On A3, the opening line about thanking the guest for their patience is good, but the next sentence feels a bit long for a busy driveway. Maybe we shorten it to something like: let me quickly check what happened so we can sort this out. That keeps it polite but faster.

In the probing section of A3, there are three questions in a row. At the door, I usually only manage one or two before the guest gets impatient. Could we mark one as essential and the others as optional examples?

For A6, on night shift, it says to call front office first for noise complaints. Often there is only one person at front desk and they are already dealing with check-ins. In practice we call security directly. Maybe the matrix should reflect that for late hours.

I like that A3 gives us some phrases to use. I am not sure about the closing line where we promise to follow up within a specific time. At the door, I do not always know how long it will take. Maybe we can say we will update them as soon as we have an answer, and then log it in A4 so the contact centre can help follow up.

On A6, for day and evening shifts, the paths look mostly right. I would just add that for serious safety concerns at the entrance, we call security first at any time, then inform front office. For billing or booking disputes, front office first makes sense. Maybe we can highlight those two categories clearly so no one hesitates.

Thanks for the detailed feedback. I will adjust A3 to shorten the opening, mark one probing question as essential and the others as optional examples, and soften the closing promise as suggested. For A6, I will change night-shift noise complaints to go to security first, and highlight that serious safety issues go to security first at any time. Once updated, I will also make sure the logging step in A4 is clearly linked so follow-up does not depend on one person remembering.

One more suggestion on A3: could we add one example for when the guest is upset about waiting for luggage at departure? That is one of our top pain points from A1, and having a standard way to acknowledge and explain while we fix it would help.
Agree on linking A3 to A4. Maybe the script can include a short line like: I will note this in our log so the team can track it, then we actually fill in A4. That way it becomes part of the habit.

For A6, on special needs guests, it currently says to call housekeeping first for equipment. In practice, we often need front office involved as well to check room allocation. Maybe the matrix should show front office as first contact, housekeeping second, with a note to involve security if there is any safety concern.

Good point. I will update A6 so that for special needs guests, front office is first contact, housekeeping second, and security is clearly marked for any safety-related concern. I will also add the luggage delay example to A3 and the line about logging in A4. Once I have made these edits, I will share a short summary and ask for a final check before we lock both A3 and A6.

Updates done. A3 now has: shorter opening, one core probing question plus optional examples, a more flexible closing, a luggage delay example, and a line about logging in A4. A6 now routes night noise to security first, highlights security first for serious safety issues, and sets front office then housekeeping for special needs, with security as needed. Can you confirm you are comfortable using these versions on shift so we can finalise T3, T4, and T6?

I have reviewed the latest A3 and A6. The script feels natural enough for the driveway and lobby, and the escalation paths match how we should act on day, evening, and night shifts. I am fine treating these as our standard going forward.
Same here. The examples in A3 cover the main situations we see, and A6 is clear enough that new team members should be able to follow it. I support using these versions in the pilot and beyond.

threads.thread_goal: Define approach for special needs guests and shift handovers before pilot.

messages.text: I have drafted A5 for special needs guest coordination and A8 for porter shift handovers, based on T5 and T12. A5 lists common scenarios like wheelchair users, visually impaired guests, families with prams, and guests with medical equipment. A8 covers open requests, stored luggage, and incidents. Can you check if these cover what you see on shift and if anything important is missing before we start the pilot?

A5 looks strong. I would add guests with cognitive difficulties or confusion, for example older guests who may get disoriented. For them, we should have a clear rule to escort them personally and inform front office and, if needed, security, especially at night.

On A5, for wheelchair users, it says to call housekeeping for ramps. In practice, we usually know where the portable ramps are stored and can bring them ourselves, then inform housekeeping. Maybe we can reflect that so we do not add extra waiting time.

For A8, could we add a line for special needs guests currently in-house, for example: guest in room 305 needs extra assistance at departure tomorrow. That way the next shift knows to plan time for it.
A8 is clear. I just want to check: do we fill it in for every shift, or only when there are open requests and incidents? I am asking because on quiet nights it might be mostly empty.

Good question. From a coordination point of view, I would say we always use A8 at least for open requests, stored luggage, and any special needs guests in-house. Even if it is short, it helps us avoid missed handovers. We can keep it simple so it does not take long to fill.

I will update A5 to add a scenario for guests who are disoriented or have cognitive difficulties, with a rule to escort them, inform front office, and involve security if there is any safety concern, in line with A6. I will also adjust the wheelchair section so we bring the ramp when we can and only call housekeeping if there is an issue.

For A8, I will add a dedicated line for special needs guests in-house, including room number, type of support, and any timing we already know, like departure. That should help the next shift plan and avoid surprises.

Sounds good. For A5, I think we should mark a few steps as non-negotiable, like always informing front office for special needs guests and logging any incidents. That way we do not skip them on busy days.

Agree. For A5, I suggest we treat these as mandatory: identify the type of support needed, inform front office, coordinate with housekeeping or security as required, and log any incidents in A4. Other details can be examples. If you are all comfortable with that, we can lock those as the core steps.
I am fine with those mandatory steps in A5. They match what we should already be doing, just written down clearly.

On A8 usage, I propose we make it standard for every shift change, even if it is short. That way we build the habit before the pilot. We can keep it to a quick list: open requests, stored luggage, incidents, and special needs guests.
That works for me. If we keep A8 short, filling it every shift should be manageable.

So to confirm: A8 will be used at every porter shift handover, with at least those four sections filled if relevant. If there is nothing to report in one section, we can just mark none. If everyone agrees, we can treat that as our standard handover rule.
Yes, I agree with that rule for A8. Using it at every handover will help us keep track of open items and special needs guests before and during the pilot.

threads.thread_goal: Plan and review the weekend pilot and training huddles outcomes.

messages.text: Sharing the plan for T7 and T8. For T7, I have set up short on-shift huddles next week to walk through A2, A3, A5, A6, A7, and A8 with all shifts. For T8, the weekend pilot will focus on the three pain points we agreed from A1: driveway greeting gaps, luggage storage and ticket mismatches, and coordination between lobby and room calls at peak times. During the pilot, we will log issues in A4 and review them in a quick daily check-in. Please confirm this focus still matches what you see on shift.

The pilot focus matches what we agreed earlier and what we see on busy weekends. I like that we are using A4 to track issues and A7 as a quick reference during shifts. For the huddles, it would help to run a short role-play on the complaint script in A3 so everyone gets comfortable using it at the door.

Agree with the focus. For driveway greeting, maybe we can set a simple rule for the pilot: if one porter is upstairs, the other stays at the entrance, and if both are busy, front office or contact centre is asked to cover. We can test that and see how many times it comes up in A4.

For luggage tickets, during the pilot I suggest we double-check that name and date are on every tag before storing, as per A2. We can note in A4 any cases where the tag did not match what was in storage so we can see if the new checklist helps.

On coordination between lobby and room calls, maybe we can agree that during the pilot we always give guests a realistic time estimate and log it in A4 when we cannot meet it. That will show us how often we over-promise.
I am ok with the pilot focus. I just want to make sure we have A7 printed at the porter station before the weekend so we can quickly check the steps if we forget something.

Yes, I will arrange printing of A7 and place copies at the porter station and contact centre desks before the pilot. For the huddles in T7, I will include a short role-play on A3 and a quick walk-through of A2 and A8 so everyone is aligned.

Quick update after the pilot weekend: we ran the huddles, used A2, A3, A5, A6, and A8 on shift, and logged 18 issues in A4. Most were about driveway greeting and luggage storage, with a few on delayed room calls. I have summarised them and will use T11 to set up a weekly review slot. Any immediate reactions from those who worked the pilot shifts?

From the pilot, I noticed that using A2 and the new tagging rule already reduced the time we spent searching for stored luggage. The complaint script in A3 also helped keep conversations calmer at the driveway. I think we should keep using both as standard, not just for the pilot.

Agree. The main gap I saw was when both porters were upstairs and no one was at the entrance. We logged those in A4. For the next weekends, maybe we can tighten the rule about asking front office or contact centre to cover the door when we know we will be away for more than a few minutes.

On the room call coordination, when we used the more flexible closing from A3 and gave realistic times, guests seemed more understanding even if we were a bit late. Logging missed times in A4 will help us see if we need more changes or just better planning.

I also found A7 useful as a quick reminder, especially for the escalation paths in A6. Maybe in the weekly review from T11 we can look at a couple of A4 entries each time and see if we followed the script and matrix or not.

Thanks for the feedback. Based on the pilot, I propose we continue focusing on the same three pain points for the next few weekends and keep using A2, A3, A5, A6, A7, and A8 as our standard tools. In the weekly T11 review, we will look at A4 entries and adjust small details if needed, but the core complaint script and focus areas stay the same.
I support that. Keeping the same focus and tools for a bit longer will give us enough data in A4 to see real trends, and the team is already getting used to A3 and the new checklists.
